title: Ang 663: the sky's aarti
hookLine: the sky as platter, sun and moon as lamps
tomorrow: if you could ask for anything, what would you ask?

cards: String lights over a backyard, a candle on every table, phone flashlights waving during the slow song. People reach for small lights when something big is happening.
On ang 663, Guru Nanak goes the other way, and answers yesterday's question. Forget the small plate of lamps. The sky is the plate.
The sun and the moon are the lamps.

teach.b: An aarti is worship with a plate of lamps, waved before the divine. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak sang this hymn at the temple in Puri, as the evening aarti began.

In paraphrase: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The sandal-scented breeze is the incense, the wind the fan, all the forests the flowers. What an aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear.
The unstruck sound is the drum.

teach.h: IN EVERYONE, THE LIGHT IS YOU.
teach.b: Then the hymn turns inward: in everyone there is light, and that light is You; by its light, everything is lit. One question for today: where is worship happening?
Guru Nanak's answer: everywhere, all the time, and in every person. Here's a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.
Psalm 19, in the King James Bible: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork."
Shared, by Jews and Christians who pray the Psalms and by Sikhs who sing this hymn: the sky isn't empty; it's praising.

One honest difference: in the Psalm the heavens speak, telling God's glory to whoever looks up. In Guru Nanak's hymn the whole sky is doing the worship itself, and then the light turns up inside every person.
Two pictures, each in its own voice, neither ranked.

how: Sikhs sing this hymn, 'gagan mai thaal', as part of Kirtan Sohila, the prayer said at night before sleep.

games.q: the sky's aarti — tap the pairs.

s: Guru Nanak's hymn and Psalm 19 say exactly the same thing
both see the sky praising. in the Psalm the heavens speak; in the hymn the sky is the worship, and the light is in everyone.
Sikhs sing this hymn at night, in Kirtan Sohila
gagan mai thaal is part of the prayer said before sleep.
the hymn's aarti is only out in the sky
it turns inward: in everyone there is light, and that light is You.

games.q: a friend from church says, 'we have a psalm like that. so it's the same thing, right?' what fits today?
o: close, not the same: the psalm's heavens speak; the hymn's sky worships.
exactly the same; every sky hymn in every religion means one thing.
nothing alike; a psalm and a Sikh hymn can't share anything.
games.why: Psalm 19: the heavens declare the glory of God. Guru Nanak: the sky is the platter, and the light is in everyone. shared, and honestly different.

practice: Find one light and look at it for the sit: the sky out a window, a lamp, a candle, even the glow of a streetlight. Keep your eyes on it softly. Before the sit ends, look once at your own hand in that light.

carryVoice: For tonight: the sky's aarti, already going, with a light in every guest. The lamps were lit long before the party.
